claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native, naturally formed surface oxide layer.
The naturally grown oxide film passivates Q235 steel at room temperature and suppresses corrosion.
Elevated-temperature exposure generates thermal stresses in the oxide film.
Thermal stresses cause cracking and delamination of the oxide film.
Cracking and delamination expose the Q235 steel substrate to the aggressive environment.
Exposure of the substrate following film failure accelerates corrosion.
Mechanical polishing removes the native oxide layer.
Controlled re-oxidation can produce a uniform and adherent oxide film on polished Q235 steel.
Oxide-film integrity, microstructure, and adhesion govern the corrosion response of Q235 steel.
A stable and uniform oxide film limits oxygen and ion ingress.
The oxide film acts as a barrier to corrosion at room temperature.
Differences in thermal expansion between the oxide film and substrate induce mechanical stress at elevated temperature.
Fresh-metal exposure caused by oxide breakdown accelerates localized corrosion.
Samples retaining a defect-free, adherent oxide film will have lower room-temperature corrosion rates than samples with damaged films.
Increasing temperature will increase oxide-film cracking or delamination.
At elevated temperature, samples with compromised oxide films will corrode faster than untreated or better-controlled re-oxidized samples.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply in corrosive environments without significant mechanical damage to the substrate.
Environmental aggressiveness and deviations from typical Q235 alloy composition may alter the corrosion response.
Absence of both elevated-temperature film damage and a corresponding corrosion-rate increase would falsify the proposed thermal-destabilization mechanism.
